title: Five Questions That Reveal Whether Your Architect Is Using AI or Faking It
author: Dr. Hernani Costa
summary_short: Real estate developers must ask five specific questions to determine whether architecture firms genuinely use AI tools or merely claim to. The questions address current AI workflows, feasibility study acceleration, measurable project outcomes, construction administration support, and strategic AI planning. Only firms that can demonstrate concrete results are worth the project fee.
summary_medium: Architecture firms increasingly claim AI readiness, but only a fraction actually deploy AI tools in their workflows. The AI in construction market reached $4.86 billion in 2025 and is projected to hit $22.68 billion by 2032, yet only 12% of construction professionals regularly use AI and 45% of organizations report zero implementation. This gap means developers are likely working with firms that could perform dramatically better but do not. The article provides five essential questions separating genuine AI adopters from firms running on manual workflows. Developers should ask how architects currently use AI in design workflows, whether they use AI to accelerate feasibility studies, if they can demonstrate measurable time or cost savings on past projects, how AI supports construction administration, and what their five-year AI strategy looks like. Firms deploying generative design platforms like TestFit, Archistar, or Autodesk's AI features report generating 2-3x more design iterations while saving over 9 hours per feasibility study. Those using AI for design rework reduction report up to 60% fewer revisions reaching construction. The five questions serve as a vendor selection framework adaptable across professional services from accounting to legal to marketing.
summary_long: The article presents a framework for real estate developers and property investors to evaluate whether architecture firms genuinely use AI tools or merely claim to. The AI in construction market reached $4.86 billion in 2025 and is projected to hit $22.68 billion by 2032, yet only 12% of construction professionals regularly use AI in specific applications and 45% of organizations report zero AI implementation. This gap between available capability and actual adoption means developers are likely working with firms that could be performing dramatically better but are not. The five questions that separate AI-ready firms from the rest address current AI usage in design workflows, acceleration of feasibility studies and test fits, demonstrable time or cost savings on past projects, AI support for construction administration and field issue reduction, and strategic vision for AI evolution over five years. Firms using tools like TestFit, Archistar, or Autodesk's AI features report generating 2-3x more design iterations while saving over 9 hours per feasibility study, and architecture firms using AI for design rework reduction report up to 60% fewer revisions reaching the construction phase. Research cited shows 10-15% project cost savings, 10-20% reduction in budget and timeline deviations, and 10-30% reduction in engineering hours through streamlined design review and estimation processes. The article argues that forward-thinking architects are positioning themselves as strategic consultants who onboard developer clients to AI feasibility tools, providing architectural expertise in zoning strategy, envelope optimization, regulatory navigation, and creative design direction where it adds the most value. The five questions adapt across professional services including accounting, legal, and marketing, serving as a procurement framework for evaluating AI readiness in any vendor selection process. The reasoning underlying this framework stems from the practical reality that most architecture firms cannot articulate specific ways AI improves their deliverables, making it difficult for developers to assess genuine capability versus marketing claims. The decision criteria embedded in the five questions force firms to demonstrate measurable improvements rather than general AI enthusiasm, protecting developers from firms that have adopted AI in name only without realizing operational benefits. The risks of selecting an AI-naive firm include slower design iteration cycles, longer feasibility study timelines, more design revisions reaching construction documents, and ultimately higher project costs driven by inefficient workflows. Operating implications for developers include the need to incorporate these questions into vendor RFIs and RFPs, establish baseline metrics for evaluating firm responses, and potentially pay premium fees for genuinely AI-capable firms that deliver measurably superior outcomes. The framework recognizes that AI adoption in architecture is not binary but exists on a spectrum, and the questions are designed to place firms along that spectrum rather than simply confirming or denying AI use.
